nameStory: The name 'spatterdock' comes from the way this plant's large leaves seem to spatter across the water's surface like paint drops on a canvas. It's also called 'cow lily' because cattle often wade into ponds to munch on its nutritious leaves and roots. The scientific name 'advena' means 'stranger' or 'foreigner,' though this native plant is anything but foreign to New England waters!
description: Spatterdock is a robust aquatic plant that creates floating carpets of heart-shaped leaves across ponds, slow streams, and marsh edges. This member of the waterlily family produces thick, leathery leaves that can grow as large as dinner plates, emerging from underwater roots called rhizomes. Unlike the showy white waterlilies, spatterdock blooms with small, globe-shaped yellow flowers that peek just above the water surface. The entire plant can spread extensively, sometimes covering large areas of shallow water.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves that float on the water surface, thick and leathery to the touch with a waxy feel. Each leaf has a deep notch where the stem attaches, creating the classic heart shape with rounded lobes.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow globe-shaped flowers about the size of a golf ball, sitting just above or at water level. The petals feel thick and waxy, and the flower has a distinctive cup or bowl shape rather than opening flat.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms extensive colonies with leaves floating on still or slow-moving water. Leaf stems emerge from thick underwater roots, and you'll often see dozens of leaves clustered together in favorable spots.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces egg-shaped green fruits that mature to brown, about the size of a small plum. The fruits split open to release seeds that float briefly before sinking, and have a slightly spongy texture.

idTips.label: Leaf Stems
idTips.description: Thick, spongy leaf stems that feel hollow and compressible when gently squeezed. These petioles emerge directly from underwater and can be quite long in deeper water.

habitat: Look for spatterdock in shallow, still or slow-moving waters throughout New England - ponds, quiet stream backwaters, marsh edges, and lake coves. It thrives in muddy bottoms rich in organic matter, typically in water 1-6 feet deep. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and arrowhead in these nutrient-rich wetland environments.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging in late spring as water warms, unfurling from tight underwater buds. Early leaves may be smaller and more reddish before developing their full green color.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full-sized floating leaves and distinctive yellow flowers blooming from June through August. This is the best time for identification when both leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin yellowing and some sink below the surface, while mature fruits may still be visible. The plant starts storing energy in its underground rhizomes for winter.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water parts die back, leaving only the thick underground rhizomes alive beneath the ice. Look for old brown stems poking through ice or dried leaves along shorelines.

funFact: Spatterdock leaves have built-in air conditioning! The large leaves create their own cooling system by pumping cool water up from the depths through their hollow stems, which can lower the leaf temperature by up to 10 degrees compared to the air - making them perfect lily pads for frogs seeking a cool spot on hot summer days.
confusionNotes: Most people confuse spatterdock with white waterlilies, but remember 'yellow and leathery' versus 'white and delicate.' Spatterdock leaves feel thick and waxy like a rubber plant, while waterlily leaves are thinner with a smooth, almost slippery surface. The flowers are the dead giveaway - spatterdock's small yellow globes versus waterlily's large white stars.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'cow lily' fool you into thinking it's related to pasture plants - this is purely about cattle behavior, not plant relationships. Spatterdock belongs to the same family as the sacred lotus and tropical waterlilies, making it part of an ancient lineage of aquatic flowering plants that has remained virtually unchanged for millions of years.
compareHints: Spatterdock is the giant of New England's yellow pond-lilies, with the largest leaves and most robust growth habit. Small yellow pond-lily has leaves typically smaller than your hand and grows in more acidic waters, while variegated yellow pond-lily has leaves with purple undersides and is much less common in our region. If you see dinner-plate sized heart-shaped leaves floating on the water, you're almost certainly looking at spatterdock.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Variegated yellow pond-lily differs from spatterdock by having smaller flowers and more pronounced leaf mottling, while small yellow pond-lily has much tinier leaves (usually under 4 inches) and grows in shallower water.
Small yellow pond-lily is much smaller in all parts compared to spatterdock, which has leaves up to a foot across and larger, more globe-shaped flowers.
